new_statements.translation: (p.17) for the tones, 1 refers to a high tone, 2 to a low tone (sandhi phenomena, inaccessible, are not taken into account): a¹ = /á/; a² = /à/ [...] (p.124) Among these one can count: a grade-III opposition [...]; a tonal opposition (high / low); [...] Tangut does not correspond to the monosyllabic tonal type, often called isolating [...] (p.210) I think the evidence presented [...] allows a definitive value to be assigned to the Tangut tones, i.e. 'high' for tone 1 and 'low' for tone 2.

new_statements.locator: Note relative a la prononciation, pdf p.17; sec. 6.1 p.124 (pdf p.175); sec. 9.2-9.2.3 pp.208-210 (pdf pp.259-261)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: copies we hold (Beaudouin 2023, Grammaire du tangoute, INALCO thesis, HAL tel-04711865, open). Checked all three locators with extracted text: (1) pdf p.17 'Note relative a la prononciation': 'pour les tons, 1 renvoie à un ton haut, 2 à un ton bas (ne tient pas compte des phénomènes de sandhi, inaccessibles) : a¹ = /á/; a² = /à/' -- verbatim. (2) sec. 6.1 p.124 (pdf 175): 'On peut dénombrer parmi ces derniers : une opposition de grade III [..]; une opposition tonale (haut / bas); [..] le tangoute ne correspond pas au type tonal monosyllabique, souvent qualifié d'isolant' -- verbatim. (3) sec. 9.2.3 p.210 (pdf 261): 'Je pense que les preuves présentées dans le premier tableau [..] permettent…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tangut (as reconstructed from the 12th-c. native rhyme dictionaries Wenhai/Tongyin and Tibetan transcriptions) is a tone language with a binary lexical tone opposition on every syllable (tone 1 平 vs tone 2 上; Beaudouin: high vs low; Gong Hwang-cherng: high-level vs rising). No modern description says anything about word stress or accent placement; the language is extinct and its prosody beyond tone class is not recoverable from the sources.
new_statements.exceptions: Beaudouin notes tone sandhi is 'inaccessible'; Hamada 2024 fn.4 cautions that the two-tone analysis is a working hypothesis inherited from the native philology; Nie (1997) proposed up to four tones (rejected by Beaudouin p.210 fn.14). Only 'accent' remarks found anywhere: Laufer 1916 pp.23-24 (speculative, diachronic, one etymology) and Miyake 2012 on pre-Tangut 'compression' (not opened).
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable/morpheme-level tone categories from rhyme dictionaries (citation forms of single characters); no word- or phrase-level prosodic description exists.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the single literary Tangut (Xixia, Mi-nyag) language of the 12th-c. rhyme dictionaries, glottocode tang1334 / ISO txg; no dialect issue. The language is extinct and known only through its script plus Tibetan/Chinese transcriptions, so any prosodic statement is a reconstruction.

new_statements.quote: (p. xvi) « pour les tons, 1 renvoie à un ton haut, 2 à un ton bas (ne tient pas compte des phénomènes de sandhi, inaccessibles) : a¹ = /á/ ; a² = /à/ » — (p.124) « le tangoute ne correspond pas au type tonal monosyllabique, souvent qualifié d'isolant, et pris comme représentatif du sino-tibétain. » — (p.210, §9.2.3) « Je pense que les preuves présentées dans le premier tableau, liées à celles présentées par Sun (2016) sur la base d'une attestation textuelle des Tangoutes parlant de leurs tons, permettent d'attribuer une valeur de contour définitive aux tons tangoute, c'est-à-dire "haut" pour le ton 1, et "bas" pour le ton 2. »
new_statements.translation: (p. xvi) 'for the tones, 1 refers to a high tone, 2 to a low tone (sandhi phenomena, which are inaccessible, are not taken into account): a¹ = /á/; a² = /à/' — (p.124) 'Tangut does not correspond to the monosyllabic tonal type, often called isolating, which is taken as representative of Sino-Tibetan.' — (p.210, §9.2.3) 'I think that the evidence presented in the first table, together with that presented by Sun (2016) on the basis of a textual attestation of the Tanguts speaking about their tones, allows a definitive contour value to be assigned to the Tangut tones, namely "high" for tone 1 and "low" for tone 2.'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (814 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Grammaire du tangoute. Phonologie et morphologie', author Mathieu Beaudouin) and its text layer. All three quoted passages found verbatim at the stated locators via extracted text on the exact pages: pdf p.17 (printed p. xvi) 'pour les tons, 1 renvoie à un ton haut, 2 à un ton bas (ne tient pas compte des phénomènes de sandhi, inaccessibles) : a¹ = /á/; a² = /à/'; pdf p.175 (printed p.124, sec. 6.1) 'le tangoute ne correspond pas au type tonal monosyllabique, souvent qualifié d'isolant, et pris comme représentatif du sino-tibétain', preceded on the same page by the list of syllable-level oppositions including 'une opposition tonale (haut /…
new_statements.relation_note: This is the same work as the one existing_statement (Beaudouin 2023, HAL tel-04711865), whose reading 'tone language, no stress statement' is confirmed by a complete read of the thesis; the catalog record (world-r2-2026-09-17) carries an empty rule, which the thesis neither fills nor contradicts. The open_url is a the Harvard library catalogue discovery landing page (JS shell) for the HAL record; the HAL document URL was re-verified today (HTTP 200, application/pdf, content-length 11815887 bytes, identical to the file held by the project downloaded 2026-09-17).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tangut is described as a two-tone language (tone 1 = high, tone 2 = low, a syllable-level opposition reconstructed from the rime dictionaries and Horpa/Tibetan correspondences); the thesis contains no statement about word stress, accent or prominence at all. A full-text search of all 814 pages for accent/stress/proéminence/tonique/atone/intensité yields no phonological hit: 'accent' occurs only as 'mettre l'accent sur' (discourse emphasis, pdf pp.474, 575, 655) and in a bibliography entry on Pattani Malay (pdf p.793); 'intensité' is Gong's vowel 'tenseness' (sec. 9.3), not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. The author notes tone sandhi is 'inaccessible' (p. xvi) and mentions one possible case of tonal sandhi in a lexicalised compound (p.496, pdf p.547); footnote 11 p.208 reports Miyake (2012) doubting that the tones were originally contour tones at all.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes the written Tangut (Xixia) language of the 11th-13th c. texts (Leilin etc.) using Gong Hwang-cherng's reconstruction, with a revised reconstruction proposed in chs. 8-9; no dialect is distinguished. Because the language is extinct and known only through rime dictionaries and transcriptions, word stress is in principle unrecoverable from the sources, which is why the phonology treats only syllable-level oppositions (tone, grade, length/gemination, rhotacisation, tenseness).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed and it was opened, so there were no listed silent/not-opened works to spot-check. As a substitute I spot-checked the other Tangut sources the reader cited as silent (all held by the project in the same folder): Gong 2020, Hamada 2024, Jacques 2003, Beaudouin 2025 and Zhang & Lai 2025 have zero stress/accent hits (Zhang & Lai's 'prominent' is non-phonological); Gong 2020 p.178-179 and Hamada 2024 p.61 state only the two tone classes. Laufer 1916 ( lines 1197-1203, printed pp.23-24) has the diachronic remark 'in Si-hia, the accent was thrown upon the first syllable' about a hypothetical disyllabic pre-form of 'camel', which the reader already reported; it is etymologic…
